Dozens of unknown MXenes found buried in materials databases (Chemistry World)

background: Start with the materials. A MAX phase is a layered ceramic with the formula \(M_{n+1}AX_n\). Here \(M\) is an early transition metal, \(A\) is a layer of a main-group element such as aluminium, and \(X\) is carbon or nitrogen. In 2011, Naguib, Gogotsi, Barsoum and colleagues at Drexel University dissolved the aluminium layers out of titanium aluminium carbide with hydrofluoric acid. What remained was a stack of atom-thin sheets, which they named MXenes. Their general formula is \(M_{n+1}X_nT_x\). The new symbol \(T_x\) stands for chemical groups (oxygen, fluorine, chlorine and others) that stick to the surfaces. A film a few millimetres thick can hold millions of such layers, so the surface area is enormous. That makes MXenes useful for batteries, electromagnetic shielding and membranes.

The open problem is search plus synthesis. Etching only works when the \(A\) layer can be removed without wrecking the rest, and it uses hazardous chemicals and a lot of water. That confines the field to a small set of MAX parents. Earlier work widened it by hand. For example, the Rosén group at Linköping University reported in 2017 an MXene with ordered vacancies. Meanwhile, records of layered carbides and halides that look MXene-like were scattered across old crystallography papers and databases. Nobody had systematically asked how many 'new' MXene chemistries were already on the shelf. Nor had anyone asked whether they could be made without etching.
articles.status: The work is peer-reviewed in Science (volume 394, issue 6823, October 29, 2026) after an August 2026 arXiv preprint. I found no independent reproduction, and the candidate and synthesis counts differ between the preprint and the journal version.
recap: Machine learning screened two big crystal databases and flagged dozens of already-made but unrecognised MXene-like compounds.
A self-igniting reaction made these layered carbides in minutes without etching or sustained heating.
The team reports 11 new rare-earth MXenes that are mostly semiconducting with varied magnetism, but independent replication is not yet reported.
deeper: Start with the materials. A MAX phase is a layered ceramic (a hard, brittle compound of metal and non-metal atoms) with formula \(M_{n+1}AX_n\). \(M\) is an early transition metal, \(A\) is a main-group element such as aluminium, and \(X\) is carbon or nitrogen. Picture a stack of sandwiches in which the \(A\) layer is the glue. In 2011 the Drexel University team dissolved that glue from titanium aluminium carbide using hydrofluoric acid. What remained were atom-thin sheets called MXenes, with formula \(M_{n+1}X_nT_x\). \(T_x\) stands for chemical groups, such as oxygen, fluorine and chlorine, that stick to the surfaces. This etching is hazardous, uses a lot of water, and works only when the \(A\) layer can be removed cleanly. So the field has stayed tied to a small set of parents.

The Linköping team, with partners in Estonia and Finland, asked a different question. How many MXene-like crystals were already recorded in old databases? They screened structures from the Materials Project and the Open Quantum Materials Database (both are public catalogues of crystal structures) against the \(M_2XT_2\) framework, which describes one \(M_2X\) layer with surface groups attached. Then they trained classifiers, models that assign each structure to a category, here "MXene-like" or "other layered material." This is triage: a cheap filter that tells chemists which records to read closely.

The preprint lists three classifiers: a support vector machine (SVM), which draws one boundary between two classes; a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a small neural network of stacked layers; and a simplified graph-based model, which treats atoms as nodes and bonds as links. I could not confirm which one produced the headline numbers.
The SVM is the simplest to write down:
\[\hat y=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf w^{\top}\phi(\mathbf x)+b).\]

This says which side of a learned boundary a crystal falls on. Here \(\mathbf x\) is a vector of numbers describing one crystal. \(\phi\) maps \(\mathbf x\) to richer features. \(\mathbf w\) is a learned weight vector with the same length as \(\phi(\mathbf x)\). \(b\) is a learned scalar offset. The \(\operatorname{sign}\) function returns \(+1\) or \(-1\). \(\hat y=+1\) means "MXene-like."

Here is a toy case with invented numbers. Let \(\phi(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x\), \(\mathbf w=(2,-1)\) and \(b=-0.5\). A crystal with \(\mathbf x=(1,0.5)\) scores \(2(1)-1(0.5)-0.5=1.0\), so \(\hat y=+1\). A crystal with \(\mathbf x=(0.1,1)\) scores \(0.2-1-0.5=-1.3\), so \(\hat y=-1\).

The screen found old records that were really MXenes. The published abstract reports 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized candidates. Chemistry World reports that seven were synthesised, including thorium nitride oxide. That is 7/33, about 21%. The preprint instead describes 38 candidates and five re-synthesised, about 13%. Treat the tallies as version-dependent.

The synthesis resembles lighting thermite. A brief ignition starts a highly exothermic reaction, one that releases heat and keeps itself going. It needs no sustained external heating and finishes within minutes, forming layered \(M_2CT_2\) phases directly. No etching of a three-dimensional parent crystal is needed.

The team then looked forward. They trained a model on the mined data to flag promising compounds that had never been made. That led to 11 unexplored rare-earth \(M_2CT_2\) MXenes, with \(M\) = Pr, Nd, Sm, Gd, Tb, Ho and Tm. Raman spectroscopy (which probes vibrations of the lattice), X-ray diffraction (which reveals the atomic stacking pattern) and density functional theory calculations agreed. Density functional theory approximates electron behaviour in a solid from quantum mechanics. Most of the new compounds were semiconducting, meaning they conduct only under certain conditions, with varied magnetic behaviour.

Compare this with earlier work. Earlier expansions, such as the 2017 Linköping MXene with ordered vacancies (planned gaps in the lattice), were widened by hand, one chemistry at a time. Here, a classifier searches the existing record, and a different synthesis route removes the dependence on etching.

The limits are clear. This is classical pattern recognition for database triage, not a frontier foundation model. The "discovery" is partly rediscovery of what the literature already held. Open questions follow. The sources disagree on counts. I could not confirm which classifier performed best. A classifier trained on known structures may also miss chemistries unlike anything already recorded.

articles.headline: Backpropagation, 1986: Teaching Every Layer of a Network Who Is to Blame
articles.dek: A 1986 paper showed how to send error signals backward through a network, so that layers hidden deep inside could learn useful features on their own.
body: The problem: a network with several layers has many weights, and only the last layer touches the answer. A weight is an adjustable number that scales a signal passing from one unit to the next. If the output is wrong, which weight deep inside deserves the blame? Earlier learning rules could adjust weights wired directly to the output but offered no principled way to train the layers in between. Those in-between layers are called hidden layers. A hidden layer is a layer between input and output whose values are not directly supervised. Without a way to train them, networks stayed shallow and limited.

The intuition: picture a factory assembly line where the final product comes out defective. The last station asks how much each of its inputs contributed to the defect. Each earlier station then asks the same question of the station before it, passing the blame backward. Every station learns how much its own settings mattered. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986), in "Learning representations by back-propagating errors" (Nature), showed this works for neural networks. They also showed that hidden units end up encoding useful internal features, which they called representations. A hidden unit is a single neuron-like element inside a hidden layer.

The vocabulary. A loss is a single number measuring how wrong the network is. A gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each weight, and it points toward steepest increase. A partial derivative says how much the loss changes when one weight is nudged and all others are held still. The chain rule says that when one quantity depends on another through a middle step, the derivatives multiply:
\[ \frac{dL}{dx} = \frac{dL}{dy}\frac{dy}{dx} \]\nThis says that a small change in x affects the loss by first changing y, and then y changing the loss. Here \(L\) is the loss (a single number), \(y\) is the middle quantity that depends on \(x\), and \(x\) is the earlier quantity we nudge. The forward pass computes outputs layer by layer. The backward pass, which is backpropagation, reuses the forward values to compute every gradient in one sweep.

The mechanism. Recall that a layer is a group of units that all process the same input together. For layer \(l\), the pre-activation (the weighted sum before the nonlinearity) is \(z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\), and the activation (the layer's output) is \(a^{(l)} = \sigma(z^{(l)})\). Here \(W^{(l)}\) is the weight matrix (outputs by inputs), \(b^{(l)}\) is the bias vector (a per-unit constant offset), \(a^{(l-1)}\) is the previous layer's output, and \(\sigma\) is a differentiable nonlinearity (a curved function that lets the network learn more than straight-line relationships) applied elementwise. Define the error signal \(\delta^{(l)} = \partial L / \partial z^{(l)}\), which says how sensitive the loss is to each unit's pre-activation. It flows backward like this:
\[ \delta^{(l)} = \left( (W^{(l+1)})^{\top} \delta^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \sigma'(z^{(l)}) \]\nIn words, each layer takes the next layer's blame, routes it back through the same weights used going forward, and scales it by the local slope \(\sigma'\). Here \(\delta^{(l)}\) is the error signal of layer \(l\) (one entry per unit in that layer), \(\delta^{(l+1)}\) is the error signal of the next layer, \(W^{(l+1)}\) is the next layer's weight matrix, and \(\sigma'(z^{(l)})\) is the slope of the nonlinearity at each unit's pre-activation. The symbol \(\odot\) means elementwise multiplication, and \(\top\) means transpose (swapping rows and columns). The weight gradient then follows:
\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} \, (a^{(l-1)})^{\top}, \qquad W^{(l)} \leftarrow W^{(l)} - \eta \, \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} \]\nA weight's gradient is its unit's blame times the input it received, and the update steps downhill. Here \(\partial L/\partial W^{(l)}\) is the gradient, a matrix with the same shape as \(W^{(l)}\), \(a^{(l-1)}\) is the input vector to layer \(l\), the arrow means "is replaced by", and \(\eta\) is the learning rate, a small positive step size.

A tiny example with no nonlinearity, so the numbers stay clear. Let \(h = w_1 x\), \(y = w_2 h\), and \(L = \tfrac12 (y-t)^2\). Here \(x\) is the input, \(h\) is the hidden value, \(y\) is the output, \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are the two weights, and \(t\) is the target. Take \(x=2\), \(w_1=0.5\), \(w_2=3\), \(t=2\). Forward: \(h=1\), \(y=3\), \(L=0.5\). Backward: \(\partial L/\partial y = y-t = 1\). Then \(\partial L/\partial w_2 = 1 \cdot h = 1\). The blame passed to the hidden value is \(\partial L/\partial h = 1 \cdot w_2 = 3\), so \(\partial L/\partial w_1 = 3 \cdot x = 6\). With \(\eta = 0.01\), the new weights are \(w_1 = 0.5 - 0.06 = 0.44\) and \(w_2 = 3 - 0.01 = 2.99\). The new forward pass gives \(h = 0.88\), \(y = 2.6312\), and \(L \approx 0.199\), down from 0.5.

What changed afterward: backpropagation became the standard way to compute gradients for networks of any depth. Today it runs inside automatic differentiation, software that records the forward computation and replays it backward to produce gradients. Transformers (attention-based language models), convolutional networks (networks that scan small filters across images), and the policies used in robotics (networks that choose a robot's actions) are all trained this way. Gradient-based optimizers, the rules that use gradients to update weights, consume its output. The core idea is unchanged from 1986. Modern work mostly makes it cheaper, more stable, and more memory-efficient.
articles.why: Nearly every deep model today, from language models to robot controllers, learns by running this backward sweep to get its gradients.
